system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-01-09 20:49:00 to 2186-01-10 17:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and chronic foot ulcers was admitted with chills and found to have gas gangrene of the right first toe. He underwent amputation and a subsequent debridement with wound vac placement. His postoperative course was complicated by sepsis, hypotension, and acute kidney injury, requiring ICU monitoring. He was treated with IV antibiotics, later transitioned to ertapenem via PICC line for six weeks. His heart failure was managed with diuresis, and his warfarin was adjusted after an elevated INR. He was stabilized and discharged to an extended care facility for ongoing IV antibiotic therapy and wound care.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Diabetes with peripheral circulatory disorders, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled
Ulcer of other part of foot
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from internal medicine. I understand you came in today because of some redness and drainage around your foot wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I took off the dressing this morning and noticed more redness than before and some yellow stuff coming out. I got worried it might be infected again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Given your history with the gas gangrene and amputation, it's smart to get it checked. We’ve reviewed your X-ray and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is it another infection? I was doing so well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — there’s no sign of a new infection. Your white blood cell count is normal, no fever, and the X-ray shows no gas or bone infection. The redness and drainage are likely from increased blood flow and healing tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But why now? I haven’t changed anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes as you start bearing more weight or moving more, the wound gets more blood flow. That can cause redness and more yellow granulation tissue — which is actually a sign of healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But the X-ray did show something about the second toe, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s flattening of the second metatarsal head — that’s called Freiberg’s infraction. It’s a stress-related change, not an infection. It may need monitoring, but it’s not causing your current symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need IV antibiotics again? I was really worried about going back on that PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think so. The podiatry team saw you and did a bedside debridement to clean up some fibrous tissue. They agree — no signs of infection. You can stay on your current oral augmentin as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So why am I being admitted then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mainly for observation and to make sure we weren’t missing anything. Since you have diabetes and a history of serious infection, we wanted to be cautious and get all the tests done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds? I stopped metformin — is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we held metformin while you're in the hospital — it's routine when there's any concern about kidney function or illness. Your creatinine is stable, though, so you can restart it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your condition is stable, and everything looks like it’s healing as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the augmentin as prescribed. Call your podiatrist this morning to schedule the skin graft — you're now a candidate since the wound is clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the redness comes back or gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly — if you develop fever, chills, increased pain, or spreading redness, come back right away. Otherwise, keep the wound clean and follow up closely with your podiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart and breathing — everything okay there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your heart rhythm is stable, oxygen levels are good, and your INR was in range. Keep taking your warfarin and metoprolol as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight? I remember last time I had to watch that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, give your doctor a call — it could be a sign of fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better knowing it’s not another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. You’ve come a long way since your last admission. Keep up the good work with your care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before discharge. All set to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got my meds, instructions, and I’ll call the podiatrist first thing tomorrow. Thank you again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and prior right hallux amputation for gas gangrene was admitted due to new erythema and yellow drainage around his surgical wound. He was evaluated for possible recurrent infection but found to have no fever, leukocytosis, or radiographic signs of osteomyelitis or soft tissue gas. The changes were attributed to benign healing changes and increased granulation tissue. Podiatry performed a bedside debridement and determined no acute surgical or infectious intervention was needed. The patient remained stable, continued on oral augmentin, and was discharged home the following day with instructions to follow up for wound grafting and monitor for signs of infection.
